then.text: Your survey is in the files, in a folder called 'The Helpful Visitor', which is a folder of one. Thank you again. The spindle whorl is a copy, by the way. The real ones are in the cupboard.
You've done all three! Jarlshof, the cliffs and the answers. Wonderful. I'll write it up: 'Visitor completed South Mainland, unsupervised, did not fall off anything.'
Here's a spindle whorl. A copy, not a real one: the real ones are over two thousand years old and not in my budget. It's a nice flat stone with a hole in it, and I'm told it's lucky.

The survey of the South Mainland. Three stops: the archaeologist at Jarlshof, the warden at Sumburgh Head with a Puffling for the cliff records, and then back to me. Take the road south. Watch for the runway.

else.text: Welcome to the Shetland Museum! Four thousand years in one building, with a shop. We're short of someone who'll walk to the south end of the Mainland and ask questions on our behalf. I'll make it worth your while.

It's a survey. At Jarlshof, the archaeologist will tell you about the oldest settlement in these islands. At Sumburgh Head, the warden will want to see a Puffling for our records. Then come back and tell me about it. Will you do it?
Take the Museum's survey?

then.text: Marvellous. South, along the road, all the way. Don't miss the sheep.

else.text: The offer stands. The museum is not going anywhere. It is, after all, a museum.

then.text: The chart? I heard. Terrible business. I was in the hall all afternoon with a plank and a flask. The shavings by the case? That's me. I'm shedding wood constantly. It's a trade hazard.

ls_boatman.text: Shetland boats are built clinker, with overlapping planks, the way the Norse did, and the old shape is still the best. Hulls like a gull in flight. These are the boats that went out to the haaf, the deep-sea fishery, and the men were out for days. Hard folk.

I build them to the old pattern. It takes a few months, and the paint is applied with great ceremony and a flask of tea. If you build a boat in Shetland you must not leave a nail to hold the wind out. I forget why, but it's an old rule.

then.text: The chart is home, and so is its copy. People are queuing to see the copy, which Marjory finds deeply unfair, and the chart finds deeply relaxing.
Edward, Prince of Wales, wore a Fair Isle pullover in public in 1921, and the fashion took off. Imagine what he'd have made of the squared paper.
That's every lead. Right. The chart was in the case at four o'clock, and by five the case was a very handsome empty box. Who took it?

else.text: Still on the trail? Take your time. The chart has waited eighty years to be stolen, it can wait a bit longer.

Elsie Nicolson, registrar. I look after the labels, the lists and my blood pressure.
A hand-painted Fair Isle chart from the 1920s has vanished from its case: borders, stars, snowflakes, the lot. No forced lock, no broken glass. Whoever took it simply walked off with it, thoroughly.

Fair Isle knitting never uses more than two colours in a row. Whoever took the chart knew that, or wanted to learn. Have a look about. Your Casebook in the Fieldbook will keep track, and a wrong accusation costs you standing.
Case opened: The Missing Chart.
